items.title: Section: Why Only Sight and Sound Carry Moral Weight, and Whether Movement Is Anything Beyond Matter Itself

items.zh: 問：眼、耳所行善不善色，彼何因緣成善等性，非餘色耶？答：若略說由軟中上品三種思差別故。一、加行思，二、決定思，三、等起思。由此能起若善不善身語表業。當知上品思為依止故，能發善不善業。問：依止聚色而有運動，當言與彼異不異耶？答：當言不異。
items.en:
Question: for what reason do the objects perceived by eye and ear alone become wholesome or otherwise, and not the remaining objects? Answer: briefly, this depends on the distinctions of weak, middling, and superior grade among three kinds of intention — preparatory, determining, and executing. These give rise to wholesome or unwholesome bodily and verbal expression. One should know it is the superior grade of intention that is capable of generating wholesome or unwholesome action.
Question: is the movement that occurs depending on a cluster of matter to be said to be different from it, or not different? Answer: it should be said not to be different.

items.zh: 何以故？於彼處所若生不生、或滅不滅而有運動，皆有過失可得故。問：有何過失？答：若言生而有動，便越剎那相；若言不生，便應無動。若言滅者，應與餘等。若言不滅，便越行相。又於異處生起因緣分明可得，是故當知無別運動實物可得。如是等類，應當思惟色蘊作業。

items.title: Section: Momentary Cessation — Why Nothing That Arises Needs a Separate Cause to Perish

items.zh: 復次，一切色蘊當言皆是剎那滅性。何以故？諸行纔生尋即壞滅，現可得故。又不應謂能生之因即是滅因，其相異故。又法生已，餘停住因不可得故。是故當知一切諸行皆任運滅。由此道理，剎那義成。
items.en: Furthermore, one should say that all form aggregate possesses the nature of momentary cessation. Why? Because conditioned phenomena, the moment they arise, immediately perish, as is directly observable. Also, one should not claim that the very cause generating something is also the cause of its ceasing, since their characteristics differ. Also, once a phenomenon has arisen, no further cause sustaining it can be found. Therefore one should know all conditioned phenomena perish spontaneously — this is how the meaning of momentariness is established.

items.title: Section: Fire Doesn't Destroy the Firewood — Refuting Every Theory of What Causes Cessation

items.zh: 若謂火等是滅壞因，不應道理。何以故？由彼火等與彼諸行俱生俱滅，現可得故。唯能為彼變異生緣，說有作用。又謂壞滅是壞滅因，不應道理。何以故？與彼俱生不應理故。若彼生時即有壞滅，便成相續斷壞過失。又唯自性滅壞說名為滅，而言能為滅因，不應道理。若言別有滅壞自性，離彼法外別有滅相畢竟不可得故，不應道理。若謂火等為滅助伴方能滅者，於燈電等及心心所任運滅中不可得故，不應道理。若謂生彼有別別功能，此差別不可得故，不應道理。若謂二種於一處所有滅功能，即應二種俱於兩分有滅功能，或無功能，有過失故，不應道理。如是等類，應當思惟色蘊剎那滅義。謂由任運壞滅因故，遮計火等為滅因故，遮計滅相為滅因故，遮計二種為滅因故。如是等類，盡當了知。又一切行是心果故，當知如心，皆剎那滅。
items.en:
To claim that fire and the rest are the cause of cessation is not reasonable. Why? Because fire and the conditioned phenomena it affects arise and cease together, as is directly observable — fire only serves as the condition for their transformation, said to have this function alone. To claim that the mark of cessation itself is the cause of cessation is likewise not reasonable. To claim that fire and the rest serve merely as an auxiliary helper to cessation is not reasonable either, since this cannot be found in the spontaneous cessation of a lamp, lightning, or mind and its mental factors. To claim that arising possesses its own distinct function is likewise not reasonable, since no such distinguishing function can be found.
Things of this kind are how form aggregate's meaning of momentary cessation should be contemplated... and furthermore, since all conditioned phenomena are mind's own product, one should know that, like mind, they too all cease moment by moment.

items.title: Section: Distinct or Not Distinct — Derived Matter Always Differs From the Elements That Produce It

items.zh: 復次，所造色於諸大種，當言有異相耶？當言無異相耶？謂有異相。何以故？異相可得故。此中異相者，謂異根所行故。所以者何？由餘色根能取大種。復由餘根取所造色故。又可運轉、不可運轉，現可得故。謂從眾花，運轉香氣置苣蕂中，世現可得，非彼堅等而可運轉。又變異、不變異，現可得故。謂煎酥等中，有色味等變異差別可得，非彼堅等。是故當知，大種、造色其相有異。
items.en: Furthermore, should derived matter be said to have a different character from the elements, or not? It should be said to have a different character. Why? Because a different character can be found. Here, "different character" means it is perceived by a different faculty... also because it can move while the elements cannot, as is directly observable... also because it changes while the elements do not, as is directly observable... one should therefore know that the elements and derived matter have different characters.

items.zh: 若於異相而執為一，於諸大種亦應爾耶？由諸大種其相展轉互相異故。若許爾者，應當唯有一大種耶？是故當知，諸所造色望彼大種，定有異相。如是等類，應當思惟諸大種色獨非獨相。復次，諸色所攝法，幾是根性？幾是所行性？謂五是根性，六是所行性。問：何等所行境是根所行耶？答：若根不壞等，如本地分中已廣說。謂由依處故，或由相故，或由方故，或由時故，或由明了、不明了故，或由全事、一分事故。問：由幾因緣，說諸根壞及不壞耶？答：由二因緣。一、由羸損故；二、由全壞故。與此相違，當知不壞。又略由四緣，諸根變異。一、由外緣所生。謂由受用攝受、損壞外境界故。或由他輩所損益故。二、由內緣所生。謂由各別不如理作意所生貪等諸纏煩惱故，或由如理作意所生三摩鉢底等故。三、由業緣所生。謂由先業增上緣力，感得端正、醜陋等故。四、由自體變異所生。謂彼諸根自相差別故。問：由幾因緣，意根壞耶？答：由四因緣。一、由蓋所作。謂於五蓋中，隨由一蓋覆蔽其心。二、由散亂所作。謂由鬼魅嬈亂其心。三、由未證所作。謂彼內心猶未證得靜慮、無色勝品功德，然於其中強發作意。四、由未解所作。謂於多聞、工巧等事心未純熟，強施方便。云何色等境界望彼諸根名為現前？

blocks.text: One of the most important arguments in Yogācāra: nothing needs a cause to perish. Everything that arises ceases by itself, moment by moment.

Master Cháng Bǎi, following the sub-commentary: preparatory, determining, and executing intentions give rise to bodily and verbal acts; only volition is truly good or bad. (Untranslated, 0600a01: how the elements lead, support, establish, sustain, and increase derived form.)

"Movement should be said not to be different from the cluster." Master Cháng Bǎi: form and sound do not reappear in the former place but arise in a new one; "movement" is a name for that. (Untranslated, 0600a11: if a thing moved while arising, it would exceed the moment; if it did not arise, there could be no movement; and the causes of arising in a new place are clearly found. So there is no separate real thing called motion.)

Three reasons: things are seen to perish as they arise; the cause of arising cannot be the cause of ceasing, since their marks differ; and no further sustaining cause can be found. Master Cháng Bǎi: arising relies on conditions; ceasing does not. 任運 means of itself, without effort.

"Fire only serves as the condition for transformation." Master Cháng Bǎi: fire makes the paper change and conditions the arising of ash; it does not destroy the paper. The treatise concludes: "all conditioned things are the result of mind, and so, like mind, they cease moment by moment."

subs.head: Derived form differs from the elements

blocks.text: They are known by different faculties; derived form can move while the elements cannot; and derived form changes while the elements do not. Master Cháng Bǎi: only the body faculty touches the elements.

If derived form were one with the elements, the elements would also have to be one, which they are not. Then: of form, five kinds are faculties and six are objects. Faculties are damaged by weakening or destruction, and change through four conditions: outer circumstances, inner afflictions or meditation, past karma, and their own nature. The mental faculty is impaired in four ways: by a hindrance covering the mind; by distraction, as when disturbed by spirits; by forcing attention towards meditative states not yet attained; and by forcing effort in learning or skills not yet mastered.
"Fire does not destroy the firewood." It sounds strange, but the claim is that change is the nature of things, not something done to them from outside.

quiz.q: The English has "three grades of intention — preparatory, determining, and executing." Is it right to equate the three grades with the three intentions?
options: yes: soft is preparatory, middle determining, and superior executing, the English matching each exactly and needing no change
no: the Chinese has only three grades, with no three intentions
no: the three are feeling, perception, and volition, which the English mistranslates
no: the three intentions raise preparatory, fundamental, and subsequent acts; soft, middle, and superior are grades of those acts, and only superior volition generates karma
quiz.why: The Sub-commentary says the preparatory, determining, and executing intentions give rise to preparatory, fundamental, and subsequent bodily and verbal acts, and these acts have the soft, middling, and superior grades; only volition joined with the superior grade generates the act. The English appositive makes the three grades and three intentions one list, which is not the structure of the passage.

quiz.q: Is the movement occurring in a cluster of matter different from it or not, and why?
options: different; movement is a separate real phenomenon added to the cluster, which is what enables it to move
neither different nor not, the treatise leaving it open
movement belongs only to mind and has nothing to do with the cluster
not different; movement is provisionally set on changes in the cluster and has no real substance
quiz.why: The treatise answers that movement should be said not to be different from the cluster. Master Cháng Bǎi: form and sound do not reappear in the place of the former moment but appear in a different place; movement is provisionally established on the changes of the cluster, with no real substance. This matches the earlier conclusion that expressed karma is provisional.

quiz.q: How does the treatise establish that all form is momentary?
options: phenomena are destroyed by outer conditions after some time, and so are called momentary in a coarse sense
because the scriptures say phenomena are impermanent, needing no further reason
because particles constantly gather and scatter
phenomena perish the moment they arise; the cause of arising is not the cause of ceasing; no sustaining cause can be found
quiz.why: The treatise gives three reasons: phenomena perish on arising, as can be observed; the cause of arising is not the cause of ceasing, since their marks differ; and no further sustaining cause can be found. Master Cháng Bǎi: between arising and ceasing nothing intervenes; arising and ceasing have no gap, there is no abiding, and so momentary cessation is proved.

quiz.q: Why is the cause of arising not the cause of ceasing, per Master Cháng Bǎi?
options: arising depends on conditions and ceasing does not; the two marks differ, so they cannot share one cause
arising and ceasing are one event, differing only in time, so they share a cause, the treatise dividing them for convenience
the cause of arising is strong and that of ceasing weak, and so they differ
the cause of arising is past and that of ceasing future
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: arising must rely on conditions, while ceasing does not rely on conditions, and the two are opposed; the marks of arising and ceasing differ, so how could they be one cause? This repeats the point of the earlier fascicle that ceasing awaits no cause.

quiz.q: The English has "perish spontaneously" for 任運滅. Is "spontaneously" apt, and how does momentariness bear on abiding?
options: it means ceasing at will, as one wishes, which "spontaneously" exactly conveys, showing a practitioner can control phenomena
it means ceasing all together, and should be "simultaneously"
it means ceasing naturally without awaiting conditions; "spontaneously" may suggest self-initiation but will serve; any slight abiding would not fit momentariness
it means ceasing slowly, and should be "gradually"
quiz.why: 任運 means without effort, of itself, not awaiting conditions. Master Cháng Bǎi: if phenomena stayed even slightly, this would not fit the meaning of momentary; and each of the views of a cause of abiding, a cause of ceasing, and natural abiding has fault. "Spontaneously" serves, though it may suggest something arising from within, whereas the Chinese simply denies an outside cause.

quiz.q: Fire turns wood to ash. Why, per Master Cháng Bǎi, is fire not the cause of ceasing?
options: fire only conditions the paper's change and the ash's arising; what is seen is ash arising, not fire destroying it
fire and wood cease in the same moment, so ash arises without cause, wholly unrelated to fire
fire is impermanent, and so has no power to burn
what burns is mind, not wood, and neither fire nor wood exists
quiz.why: The treatise says fire only serves as the condition for transformation. Master Cháng Bǎi: fire merely makes the paper change and conditions the arising of ash; it is not a condition that destroys the paper, so ceasing awaits no condition. What one sees is fire turning paper to ash, with ash existing; it is not that nothing remains.

quiz.q: "Since all conditioned phenomena are mind's product": what follows?
options: when mind ceases, phenomena continue for a while, form lasting longer than mind
like mind, they all cease moment by moment
phenomena are made by mind, so no practice is needed
mind is permanent, and so phenomena are permanent
quiz.why: The treatise closes its case: all conditioned phenomena are the result of mind, and so, like mind, they cease moment by moment. Master Cháng Bǎi: form is manifested from mind, and one should know that like mind and mental factors it is momentary. Lamps, lightning, and mental states were the examples of ceasing without an outside cause.

quiz.q: Why does derived matter have a different character from the elements?
options: the elements are larger, derived matter being cut from them, and size is the only difference
the elements are mental and derived matter form
they are perceived by different faculties; derived matter moves and the elements do not; it changes and they do not
the treatise holds them to have no difference, only different names
quiz.why: The treatise gives three grounds: they are perceived by different faculties, derived matter can move while the elements cannot, and derived matter changes while the elements do not. Master Cháng Bǎi: only the body faculty takes the four elements, while eye, ear, nose, and tongue take derived matter; derived matter can be moved, the elements as such cannot.

quiz.q: The verse's 獨 is "solitary nature," and the overview says "Solitary or Accompanied." According to the lecture, what is 獨?
options: 獨 means derived matter existing alone, apart from the elements, so "Solitary" is exactly right and needs no comparison
獨 means pratyekabuddhas, referring to form in their domain
獨 means having a different character, and 非獨 not having one; it does not mean alone or accompanied
獨 means mental consciousness acting alone in taking form
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: 獨相 means having a different character, and 非獨相 means having none. The heading in the verse thus announces the discussion of whether derived matter differs in character from the elements. The English "solitary nature" and the overview's "one kind alone, or always accompanied" take the word literally and miss what the section is about.
